Financial Econometrics · Multivariate Analysis

Factor
Models

From many observed time series to a few latent forces.

01 · Common variation

What moves commodity markets together?

Monthly commodity prices with complete observations from January 2000 to December 2025. Prices have different units: rebase them to 100, then calculate monthly log returns.

Can a few latent variables summarize these movements?

\[x_t=\Lambda f_t+e_t\]

Common components capture shared movements; idiosyncratic components capture variation not explained by the selected factors.

Principal component analysis

Step 1 · Standardize the series

Subtract each series' mean and divide by its standard deviation so that volatile commodities do not dominate simply because of their scale.\[z_{it}=(x_{it}-\bar x_i)/s_i\]

Step 2 · Look for common variation

Calculate pairwise correlations of standardized monthly returns. Positive correlations indicate that prices tend to move together.

Step 3 · Construct the first factor

Find a weighted combination of the standardized series that captures as much variation as possible. Normalize the weights so their squared sum is one.\[f_{1t}=w_1z_{1t}+\cdots+w_Nz_{Nt},\qquad \sum_i w_i^2=1\]

Additional factors

Extract further factors that are orthogonal (uncorrelated in the sample) to the preceding factors and explain as much of the remaining variation as possible.

Interpreting the PCA output

The individual bars show how much of total standardized variation each factor explains. The cumulative line shows how much is captured jointly.

Loadings describe the direction and relative weight of each commodity in a factor. A broadly positive first factor suggests a common commodity-market movement. Factor signs are arbitrary.

A common commodity price factor is not automatically global demand: supply shocks and financial conditions can also drive common movements.
02 · Back to the yield curve

We already know three factors.

Nelson–Siegel imposed economically motivated loadings. What if we let the data choose them?

Monthly Treasury yields from FRED. PCA uses months with all eleven maturities available, centering yield levels without standardizing them because they share the same units. This describes historical curve variation, not necessarily stationary shocks.

Compare shapes rather than magnitudes: PCA estimates normalized loadings from the data, while Nelson–Siegel imposes functional shapes. PC1 resembles level, PC2 slope and PC3 curvature. Signs are aligned for comparison.

03 · Factor dynamics

From static to dynamic factor models

We previously learned in Mean Reversion that the level, slope and curvature of the yield curve have time dynamics. We modeled them with an AR(1) process.

\[f_t=c+\phi f_{t-1}+u_t\]

So far, we have estimated a static factor model. We can now specify a dynamic factor model, jointly describing the observations and the evolution of the latent factors.

\[\begin{aligned}y_t&=\Lambda f_t+\varepsilon_t &&\text{Measurement equation}\\ f_t&=c+Af_{t-1}+u_t &&\text{State equation}\end{aligned}\]

Here \(\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,R)\) and \(u_t\sim N(0,Q)\). PCA alone can no longer estimate this joint dynamic model: it does not use the time ordering of observations. We need a state-space approach.

04 · State-space models

How do we estimate something we cannot observe?

The Kalman filter

Consider a scalar latent AR(1) observed with noise, with independent Gaussian innovations. For this centered example the intercept is zero.

\[f_t=\phi f_{t-1}+u_t,\quad y_t=f_t+\varepsilon_t,\quad u_t\sim N(0,Q),\quad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,R)\]

1 · Start with yesterday's information

\(m_{t-1}=\hat f_{t-1|t-1}\) is our latest state estimate; \(P_{t-1}\) is its estimation-error variance.

2 · Predict today's state

\[a_t=\hat f_{t|t-1}=\phi m_{t-1}\] The AR(1) equation gives our best prediction before seeing today's observation.

3 · Predict the uncertainty

\[P_t^-=\phi^2P_{t-1}+Q\] Previous uncertainty propagates through the AR(1), and a new state shock adds uncertainty. Predict the observation as well: \[\hat y_{t|t-1}=a_t,\qquad S_t=P_t^-+R\] The observation prediction error contains both state uncertainty and measurement noise. The Kalman gain is the share attributable to state uncertainty: \[K_t=\frac{P_t^-}{P_t^-+R}\]

4 · Observe and update

We observe \(y_t\). The prediction error is \(v_t=y_t-\hat y_{t|t-1}\). Attribute a fraction of this surprise to the latent state: \[m_t=a_t+K_tv_t\] Our uncertainty also decreases: \[P_t=(1-K_t)P_t^-\] Repeat the process next period.

Explore one prediction and update

Repeat the filter over time

From filtering to maximum likelihood

The innovation is \(v_t=y_t-a_t\), with variance \(S_t=P_t^-+R\). The filter evaluates the likelihood one observation at a time.

\[\ell(\theta)=-\frac12\sum_t[\log(2\pi)+\log S_t+v_t^2/S_t]\]

Maximize this likelihood over the unknown parameters. In the multivariate case, the gain becomes \(K_t=P_t^-\Lambda'(\Lambda P_t^-\Lambda'+R)^{-1}\).

05 · US economic activity

Extracting a latent business-cycle indicator

Five FRED monthly indicators, transformed into standardized log growth rates.

IndicatorFRED ticker
Industrial productionINDPRO
Nonfarm payroll employmentPAYEMS
Real personal income excluding transfersW875RX1
Real manufacturing and trade salesCMRMTSPL
Real personal consumption expendituresPCEC96
\[\begin{pmatrix}z_{production,t}\\z_{employment,t}\\z_{income,t}\\z_{sales,t}\\z_{consumption,t}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}h_1\\h_2\\h_3\\h_4\\h_5\end{pmatrix}f_t+\varepsilon_t,\qquad f_t=\phi f_{t-1}+u_t\]\[R=\operatorname{diag}(r_1,\ldots,r_5),\qquad Q=1\]

Fix Q to identify the factor scale and assume contemporaneously uncorrelated measurement errors. Estimate the remaining parameters by maximum likelihood.

Estimated model parameters

Loadings measure sensitivity to the common factor, measurement variances describe idiosyncratic noise, and the AR coefficient describes persistence.

Standardize both factors to compare their fluctuations rather than their arbitrary scales.

Filtering uses observations through t, while smoothing also uses later observations. Both use parameters estimated over the full sample here.

From monthly activity to quarterly GDP

The quarterly average of the filtered factor is compared with real GDP quarterly log growth over the common sample. This is a retrospective comparison, not a real-time nowcast.

Can we extract a monthly indicator of aggregate economic activity without directly observing monthly GDP?
